deep.reconstruction:
This page holds no derivation. It is one month (June, rows 1–31; row 31 = July 1, repeated as the first line of the next page) of a computed daily table for reducing star places. The 'Junius' header is visible. The ♈ (first point of Aries) mark appears on the previous page, not here. I identified the ten columns from the numbers alone; the identifications are mine, but each was checked against several rows.

(0) Row index: the day.

(4) L = true longitude of the Sun from the equinox, in deg.min.sec.
- 71°31'58" on June 1, passing 90° between June 20 and 21 (the solstice).
- Daily differences fall from 57'15" to 57'02".

(1) τ = elapsed fraction of the tropical year.
- It grows uniformly by 0.00273 per row (0.4184 → 0.5003 in 30 rows).
- That is 1/366.2 year, i.e. one sidereal day, not one mean solar day (1/365.24 = 0.002738).
- This fits column 4: the Sun's true motion near aphelion is about 57'11" per solar day; times 0.99727 this gives about 57'02" per sidereal day, as tabulated.
- So the entries are spaced at sidereal-day intervals, plausibly at each culmination of ♈ (sidereal 0h); the ♈ on the previous page points the same way.
- Origin of τ (my computation): mean anomaly ≈150°, equation of centre ≈ +0.95°, so the mean longitude on June 1 ≈ 70.58°. Going back 0.4184 × 360° = 150.6° gives a mean longitude of ≈280.0° at τ = 0. That is the 'annus fictus' start (mean Sun at 280°) later standard with Bessel.

(2) A = τ + (solar nutation in longitude)/(annual precession).
- Empirically A − τ ≈ −0.0199·sin2L. Examples: −0.0198 at L = 41.8° (May 1); −0.0120 on June 1; ≈0 at the solstice; +0.0194 at L = 128.6° (July 32).
- 0.0199 × 50.2" ≈ 1.0" sin2L, i.e. a solar nutation in longitude of about 1.0".
- Only the solar term appears, so the lunar (node) terms must be tabulated separately.

(3) B = solar nutation in obliquity with reversed sign, ≈ −0.43"·cos2L.
- Values: −0.05 (May 1), +0.35 (June 1), +0.43 (solstice), +0.10 (July 31).
- The ratio 1.0/0.43 ≈ 2.3 matches the theoretical ratio for the solar term (modern 1.32/0.57), though both coefficients are about 0.75 of the modern ones.

(5), (6), (7) Aberration day numbers with k ≈ 20.61".
- Column 5 = C·tanε = −k sinε cosL. June 1: −20.61 × 0.3983 × 0.3168 = −2.600.
- Column 6 = C = −k cosε cosL. June 1: −5.99.
- Column 7 = D = −k sinL. June 1: −19.548; at the solstice −20.61.
- ε ≈ 23°28'.

(8), (9) Polar ('star constant') form of the aberration day numbers.
- Definition: h sinH = C, h cosH = D, so that Δα·cosδ = h sin(H+α) = C cosα + D sinα.
- June 1: arctan(5.99/19.55) = 17.04°, so H = 197°2'; h = √(5.99² + 19.55²) = 20.447, log h = 1.31063 → 1.3106.
- June 30: H = 180° − arctan(3.00/20.35) = 171°37'; log h = log 20.570 = 1.3132.
- In closed form: tan(H−180°) = cosε·cotL, and h = k√(sin²L + cos²ε cos²L).
- H decreases about 53' per day near the solstice, since dH/dL = −cosε there. log h peaks at log 20.61 = 1.3141, symmetric about L = 90°.

The purpose is a working table of Besselian-type day numbers (τ, A, B, C·tanε, C, D, H, log h) for daily reduction of meridian observations of stars, with the solar terms only.
errors: June 7, column 1 reads 0.4357 in the transcription, but the uniform sequence requires 0.4347 (0.4320, 0.4347, 0.4375). This is either a slip by Gauss or a misreading.
June 14, column 2 = 0.4498 against a model value of 0.4497. Its neighbours' differences (35, then 32) are uneven; this is at most a last-digit rounding wobble.

The aberration constant implied by every column is about 20.61" (log h max = 1.3141). This is not Delambre's/Bessel's 20.255" nor Struve's 20.445"; its source is unclear (no arithmetic error, just an unusual constant).
The solar nutation coefficients implied (≈1.0" in longitude, ≈0.43" in obliquity) are about 25% below modern values (1.32", 0.57"). This reflects period theory or constants, not a slip.
Otherwise all spot checks (June 1, 10, 15, 20, 21, 30) agree to the last tabulated digit.

results.what: Daily solar longitude and fraction of the tropical year τ, with entries spaced at sidereal-day intervals (Δτ = 1/366.24); τ counted from the moment the mean Sun is at 280°.
results.modern_name: Besselian fictitious year (annus fictus) and τ argument of the day numbers
results.usually_credited_to: F. W. Bessel (Fundamenta Astronomiae 1818; Tabulae Regiomontanae 1830)

results.what: Solar parts of the nutation day numbers: A − τ ≈ −0.0199 sin2L and B ≈ −0.43" cos2L.
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers A, B (solar nutation terms)
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (day-number formalism); solar nutation theory from d'Alembert and Laplace

results.what: Aberration day numbers C = −k cosε cosL, D = −k sinL and C·tanε, with k ≈ 20.61".
results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers C, D (annual aberration)
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel; aberration discovered by Bradley in 1729

results.what: Polar form of the aberration: h sinH = C, h cosH = D, giving the aberration in right ascension as h sin(H+α) sec δ; tabulated as H and log h.
results.modern_name: Bessel's star-constant form (h, H) of the aberration reduction
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (Tabulae Regiomontanae 1830); similar auxiliary-angle forms in Zach's aberration/nutation tables (1806)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computed ephemeris of reduction day numbers. Gauss's interest in practical star reduction is well known. The only mildly notable features are the sidereal-day spacing, the τ origin at mean longitude 280° (Bessel's annus fictus), the polar (h, H) form, and the unusual constant k ≈ 20.61". These would matter only if the page could be dated before Bessel's 1818/1830 publications, and nothing on the page dates it.
